profiles.title: War and Peace
profiles.author: Leo Tolstoy
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic and historical statements checked against individually listed sources. Original interpretations are explicitly editorial. No full-text audit, exhaustive trigger list, exact reader copy or cover verification.

publication.basis: Serialization began 1865; substantially revised first book form 1869 (UPenn work-level bibliography).

profiles.genre_and_form: Russian historical novel, polyphonic family saga and philosophical inquiry

series.name: Standalone work
series.sequence_status: No numbered fictional series applies to this work.

profiles.summary: Against the Napoleonic wars, Tolstoy interweaves the lives of several Russian families with military campaigns, courtship, grief, spiritual change and the difficult search for a meaningful life. Pierre, Natasha and Prince Andrei are among the figures whose private decisions meet a history nobody fully controls. Its recurring historical reflections challenge the notion that a handful of celebrated commanders explain enormous collective events.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The text first appeared in installments starting in 1865 and in a substantially revised book form in 1869; these are not identical publication objects. The user’s chosen Oxford World’s Classics reading path uses Louise and Aylmer Maude’s translation revised and edited by Amy Mandelker (the publisher lists ISBN 9780199232765). Modern scholarship also explores how this fictional account shaped public memory of 1812, rather than accepting every event as a documentary record.
profiles.before_reading: Keep a gentle, growing list of character names and relationships, but do not force every family relation into memory in week one. Mark a second type of note for the narrator’s claims about causation and historical greatness; compare them with actual choices made by people in scenes. Use the morning chapter ritual as a long conversation, not a race.
profiles.literary_approach: Tolstoy moves between intimate psychological observation, social scenes, battlefield uncertainty and direct arguments about history. Frequent shifts of scale make individual action feel consequential and also radically limited. The original work’s Russian and French language layers, and the Maude/Mandelker editorial treatment of them, can change a reader’s perception of class and voice.
profiles.context: The action involves Russia and Napoleon’s campaigns, but the novelist did not set out to write a neutral military history. A scholarly treatment of War and Peace as historical novel explains its contribution to cultural memory. The 2026 Footnotes & Tangents schedule is deliberately mapped onto 2027; publisher facts about the novel and the host’s interpretation of daily chapters are distinct sources.

themes.label: Ordinary life within history
themes.discussion: Domestic vulnerability and political catastrophe keep colliding.

themes.label: Great person theory
themes.discussion: The novel questions how much power famous commanders can really exercise.

themes.label: Change over long time
themes.discussion: A slow read permits values and characters to be revisited months later.

profiles.personal_fit: Strong fit for yearlong reflective reading, beautiful psychological prose and Russian history alongside Dostoevsky; one morning chapter can become a low-pressure philosophical exercise.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The scale, many names, essay-like passages and changing narrative rhythms can be frustrating if a reader expects each chapter to end with a plot hook. Long spans are not a reason to mark the daily ritual failed.

notes: War and battlefield deaths, injury and civilian suffering feature in the historical setting; intensity is not fully audited.
Marriage, grief, illness and social hierarchy receive recurring attention.

reading_questions: What seemingly small decision changes a relationship today?
Who claims to understand the war, and how would that knowledge be tested?
What does the narrator let you notice that a historical timeline would miss?
discussion_questions: What counts as agency when history is larger than any individual?
When does a fictional portrayal become part of how a culture remembers its past?

related_connections.note: Compare Tolstoy’s moral development through social networks with Dostoevsky’s close interrogation of guilt.

related_connections.label: Aristotle’s ethics
related_connections.note: Contrast a life of flourishing and deliberate choices with Tolstoy’s historical pressure.

profiles.title: The New Jim Crow
profiles.author: Michelle Alexander
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic and historical statements checked against individually listed sources. Original interpretations are explicitly editorial. No full-text audit, exhaustive trigger list, exact reader copy or cover verification.

publication.basis: First publication 2010; tenth-anniversary New Press edition 2020 with a new preface (publisher and library).

profiles.genre_and_form: Nonfiction; legal and political argument about U.S. punishment and racial inequality

series.name: Standalone work
series.sequence_status: No numbered fictional series applies to this work.

profiles.summary: Michelle Alexander argues that ostensibly race-neutral criminal-justice rules can recreate durable racial exclusion, particularly through policing, prosecution, incarceration and post-conviction restrictions on employment, housing and civic participation. The phrase “new Jim Crow” is an analogy about a linked system of disadvantage; it is the author’s historical thesis rather than a claim that the statutes and eras are identical.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Originally published in 2010, the New Press issued a tenth-anniversary edition in 2020 with Alexander’s new preface. Her advocacy and policy analysis profoundly influenced public discussion of mass incarceration. James Forman Jr.’s 2012 NYU Law Review article praises the attention paid to injustice but contests the historical analogy as too centered on drugs, insufficiently attentive to violence, class variation and other affected communities.
profiles.before_reading: Separate three columns as you read: documented statute or study, Alexander’s causal interpretation, and a question requiring updated evidence. Note dates on prison population figures: an observed trend before 2010 is not automatically current in 2027.
profiles.literary_approach: Alexander builds a system-level case by moving between legal mechanisms, historical comparisons, public rhetoric and cumulative consequences after a sentence. The rhetoric of an analogy creates moral urgency but invites testing where two historical arrangements differ.
profiles.context: The book intervened in debates on the drug war, felon disenfranchisement and civil rights. Independent criminological scholarship has since expanded the history of the carceral state. Scholars disagree over how useful and complete the Jim Crow analogy is, while acknowledging the need to analyze racialized punishment. This profile does not adjudicate current numerical claims.

themes.label: Civil exclusion
themes.discussion: Sentencing is not the only possible long-term penalty when civil opportunities remain restricted.

themes.label: Analogy as method
themes.discussion: Historical comparison can reveal structural patterns and also erase dissimilarities.

themes.label: Reform and evidence
themes.discussion: A compelling moral frame still requires updated statistics and explicit mechanisms.

profiles.personal_fit: Likely rewarding for a reader who values research literacy, ethical argument, and separating claims from evidence; pairs well with Caste and The Sum of Us without assuming they agree on every mechanism.
profiles.possible_mismatch: Polemic urgency and sweeping comparisons are not a substitute for time-specific empirical estimates; readers should treat pre-2020 data as historical, not automatically the latest situation.

notes: Discussion of racial discrimination, state violence, criminal convictions, imprisonment and poverty.
This is not a comprehensive trauma-content review; statistics or policy changes after 2020 may materially alter an example.

reading_questions: Which chapter gives the clearest concrete mechanism for an exclusionary outcome?
Is the evidence correlational, causal, historical or legal?
What data year is attached to a striking claim?
discussion_questions: Does the historical analogy clarify remedies or obscure relevant differences?
How does Forman’s critique alter the questions you would ask without dismissing Alexander’s underlying concern?

related_connections.note: Compare system-level metaphors and what each can or cannot reveal.

related_connections.note: Compare punishment-focused mechanisms with policy coalitions and public goods.

profiles.title: Making Money
profiles.author: Terry Pratchett
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic and historical statements checked against individually listed sources. Original interpretations are explicitly editorial. No full-text audit, exhaustive trigger list, exact reader copy or cover verification.

publication.basis: Verified publisher/library work-level date; editions and translated texts may carry separate dates.

series.name: Discworld — Moist von Lipwig novels
series.sequence_status: Moist’s central sequence: Going Postal (2004), Making Money (2007), Raising Steam (2013). Discworld is a shared world with overlapping characters; these are not its only relevant books.

profiles.summary: Moist von Lipwig, ex-con man and reluctant public servant, moves from rescuing the Post Office to the far stranger work of the Royal Mint and a bank. The apparently respectable financial establishment turns out to depend on habits, theatrical authority and dubious assumptions. Cash, confidence and public trust drive the jokes as surely as the characters do.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Pratchett’s official book page lists Making Money in September 2007. The official sites for Going Postal and Raising Steam support Moist’s earlier and later appearances. Treat the three-book Moist path as a reading sequence within Discworld, not evidence that the author’s entire fictional universe follows one straightforward chronology.
profiles.before_reading: Watch how characters treat a coin, a promise and a reputation as different kinds of value. Recall the postal institution without assuming the plot of its predecessor is being summarized here; many of the pleasures come from seeing a familiar confidence trick applied to a new public system.
profiles.literary_approach: Satire runs through deliberately absurd job descriptions, brisk dialogue, bureaucratic inversions and invented institutional detail. Pratchett uses an ex-fraudster as a lens through which official finance can appear both respectable and suspicious.
profiles.context: Ankh-Morpork is a comic invented city, not a reliable account of real banking law. Its jokes about financial trust can prompt questions about money as social agreement, but any connection to a specific historical banking crisis is a reader’s interpretation rather than a documented author intention.

themes.label: Trust and currency
themes.discussion: Money is useful partly because communities agree to treat it as valuable.

themes.label: Useful dishonesty
themes.discussion: Moist’s talent for persuasion can aid public institutions or manipulate them.

themes.label: Institutional theater
themes.discussion: Authority depends on repeated performances as well as rules.

profiles.personal_fit: A fun change of pace after dense ethical or historical nonfiction while still providing sharp ideas about commerce and institutions.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The crowded cast, running Discworld in-jokes and slapstick may not satisfy a reader wanting one relentlessly serious philosophical debate.

notes: Comic peril, assassination threats and institutional corruption appear in the official publisher premise.
No exhaustive chapter-level content audit was performed.

reading_questions: Where does an honest-sounding transaction rely on confidence rather than evidence?
When is Moist exploiting a rule, and when is he improving it?
What would the bank be without its human relationships?
discussion_questions: Does a morally questionable protagonist become trustworthy through results or intentions?
Which absurdity has the clearest real-world counterpart, and where does analogy break?

related_connections.note: Continue Moist’s public-institution journey into transport and technology.

related_connections.label: Kant’s Groundwork
related_connections.note: Compare an outcome-based trust test with a duty-based account of honest action.

profiles.title: The Enchiridion
profiles.author: Epictetus
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic and historical statements checked against individually listed sources. Original interpretations are explicitly editorial. No full-text audit, exhaustive trigger list, exact reader copy or cover verification.

publication.basis: Ancient philosophical teaching transmitted by Arrian, likely early imperial era; no reliable precise publication year to enter as a modern imprint.

profiles.genre_and_form: Ancient Stoic ethical handbook, transmitted through Arrian

series.name: Standalone work
series.sequence_status: No numbered fictional series applies to this work.

profiles.summary: The Enchiridion, also known as the Handbook, is a compact selection of practical Stoic teachings associated with Epictetus. It begins by distinguishing what is properly within one’s power—such as judgment and choice—from external events, reputation and fortune. Later precepts apply that distinction to emotions, desire, criticism, relationships and disciplined attention.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Epictetus taught in the Roman imperial world but did not author a modern published book. His pupil Arrian recorded the Discourses and distilled a shorter Handbook from the teaching tradition; exact transmission and dating require caution. Oxford World’s Classics publishes Robin Hard’s translation of Discourses, Fragments, Handbook with Christopher Gill’s introduction, a modern example rather than a verified edition owned by the reader.
profiles.before_reading: Try each maxim as a question, not a self-punishing command: What is actually within my influence in this situation, and what is not? Mark when a strict passage seems to leave too little room for grief or social obligations, and return after reading a Discourses explanation.
profiles.literary_approach: Aphoristic compression makes the book useful for short reading sessions but easy to misread as slogan. Stoic vocabulary surrounding impressions and prohairesis carries more nuance than a loose English expression such as “control your feelings.”
profiles.context: The Handbook belongs to ancient Stoic ethics, shaped by ideas of judgment, character and freedom under constraint. The Stanford Encyclopedia outlines how Epictetus’ teaching survived through Arrian and later traditions; alternative translations can shift terms such as choice, will, and what is up to us.

themes.label: Judgment and external events
themes.discussion: The important distinction is agency over judgment rather than denial of external injustice.

themes.label: Training attention
themes.discussion: Ethical life becomes repeated correction of impressions rather than one decisive insight.

themes.label: Freedom under constraint
themes.discussion: A person can question what kind of freedom remains when circumstances cannot be chosen.

profiles.personal_fit: A direct, aphoristic complement to longer Aristotle and Kant readings; manageable alongside the morning/evening slow reads.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The brevity can conceal disagreement about translation, political obligation and emotionally healthy responses to harm. Avoid treating the book as an instant mental-health prescription.

notes: Death, loss, injury and external deprivation appear in Stoic examples; exact English wording varies with the translator.
Read as philosophical history, not contemporary clinical guidance.

reading_questions: Where is the line between judgment and circumstance in this passage?
Would the advice change if another person’s safety were at stake?
Which Greek philosophical term seems over-neat in English?
discussion_questions: Can Stoic acceptance coexist with activism or moral protest?
How does Epictetus differ from Aristotle on flourishing when resources are scarce?

related_connections.label: Nicomachean Ethics
related_connections.note: Different accounts of virtue, circumstances and practical flourishing.

related_connections.label: Groundwork
related_connections.note: Compare Stoic rational agency with Kantian duty.

profiles.title: Caste
profiles.author: Isabel Wilkerson
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic and historical statements checked against individually listed sources. Original interpretations are explicitly editorial. No full-text audit, exhaustive trigger list, exact reader copy or cover verification.

publication.basis: Verified publisher/library work-level date; editions and translated texts may carry separate dates.

profiles.genre_and_form: Narrative history and social criticism using comparative analogy

series.name: Standalone work
series.sequence_status: No numbered fictional series applies to this work.

profiles.summary: Isabel Wilkerson proposes that a persistent hierarchy of social rank is a way to understand racial subordination in the United States. She uses “caste” as a lens to connect U.S. racial orders, the Indian caste tradition and Nazi Germany, alternating historical narrative, anecdote and structural metaphor. The book asks readers to look beneath individual prejudice toward enduring rules of social placement.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Caste was published by Random House in August 2020. The Harvard Kennedy School library situates its thesis as a portrait of social hierarchy. Its comparative framework is debated: scholars of South Asian history and stratification challenge the equivalence of caste and race, and an Oxford Review of Economic Policy discussion notes alternative long-standing accounts such as Oliver Cox’s.
profiles.before_reading: Record each comparison in two parts: the structural feature Wilkerson hopes to reveal and the differences the comparison may conceal. Do not collapse India’s caste history, Nazi persecution and American racial slavery into a single identical experience; attend to chronology and each society’s specificity.
profiles.literary_approach: Wilkerson relies on extended metaphor, history, vignette and an architectural image of hidden beams. The book’s emotional and rhetorical force can be evaluated separately from how well the comparative analogy establishes causal explanations.
profiles.context: Whether “caste” is the best explanatory frame for American racial hierarchy is a live scholarly question. Independent debate considers the respective histories of caste, race and class. The author’s framework is not a substitute for consulting historians of the specific societies compared.

themes.label: Hidden structure
themes.discussion: Focus shifts from personal prejudice to persistent institutional positioning.

themes.label: Comparative analogy
themes.discussion: Comparisons can illuminate one dimension while obscuring others.

themes.label: Hierarchy and repair
themes.discussion: Acknowledging inherited rules is different from assigning inherited individual guilt.

profiles.personal_fit: Well matched to a reader interested in moral psychology, history, systems and careful comparative reasoning; creates worthwhile tension with The New Jim Crow.
profiles.possible_mismatch: Some broad analogies are contested by scholars; treat sweeping claims with a separate evidence-check rather than reading publisher praise as definitive confirmation.

notes: Historical descriptions of enslavement, racial terror, discrimination and Nazi violence may be distressing.
No comprehensive page-by-page content or factual-claim audit has been completed.

reading_questions: What precisely does “caste” explain in this chapter that “racism” does not?
Which societies are compared and what remains different?
Where is an anecdote supporting a claim versus illustrating it?
discussion_questions: Is a conceptual analogy helpful even when it is not exact?
What additional sources would you consult before claiming any one hierarchy explains another?

related_connections.note: Two system-level accounts of contemporary racial hierarchy with different emphases.

related_connections.label: The Sum of Us
related_connections.note: Contrast hierarchy diagnosis with a theory of solidarity and public goods.

profiles.title: The Obelisk Gate
profiles.author: N. K. Jemisin
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic and historical statements checked against individually listed sources. Original interpretations are explicitly editorial. No full-text audit, exhaustive trigger list, exact reader copy or cover verification.

publication.basis: Verified publisher/library work-level date; editions and translated texts may carry separate dates.

profiles.genre_and_form: Epic science fantasy; Broken Earth trilogy, second volume

series.name: The Broken Earth
series.sequence_status: Second of three main novels; follows The Fifth Season and precedes The Stone Sky. Read with the first book’s discoveries in mind; this preview does not reveal them.

profiles.summary: In a world repeatedly shaken by catastrophic seasons, the surviving characters must navigate threatened communities and powerful earth-altering capacities. Essun’s search and the dangers surrounding her missing daughter continue, while what seemed certain about this world becomes less secure. The book advances the trilogy’s central questions without a self-contained fresh starting point.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Orbit released The Obelisk Gate in 2016 as the second book in N. K. Jemisin’s Broken Earth trilogy. Publisher listings clearly place it after The Fifth Season and before The Stone Sky; the trilogy’s recognition across three Hugo Award years belongs to the published series history, not to an invented reader-specific edition.
profiles.before_reading: Before opening, consider a spoiler-free reminder of what you personally remember from The Fifth Season rather than reading an internet plot recap. Pay attention to who controls the explanation of geological danger and whose testimony is dismissed.
profiles.literary_approach: Jemisin extends the original book’s layered revelation structure and deliberately constrained access to knowledge. Changing perspectives and unusual magic/science systems make the ethical questions inseparable from the worldbuilding.
profiles.context: The fictional social organization and environmental catastrophe should be read as an invented system that offers room to think about oppression, parenthood, knowledge and survival, not as a one-to-one scientific account of geophysics.

themes.label: Knowledge and authority
themes.discussion: What people think they understand shapes the choices they permit themselves.

themes.label: Survival and solidarity
themes.discussion: The conditions for collective safety challenge isolated moral perfection.

themes.label: Inheritance and family
themes.discussion: Parent-child relationships exist within institutional constraints.

profiles.personal_fit: A strong fit for immersive, layered fantasy with moral complexity; rewarding if The Fifth Season’s unusual viewpoint and thematic intensity appealed.
profiles.possible_mismatch: A genuine sequel with high emotional intensity: starting here without the first book can expose major prior-book revelations and make the structure confusing.

notes: Publisher material indicates mortal danger and a parent searching for a missing child.
A complete accounting of violence, trauma or other sensitive material has not been verified.

When does protecting someone become controlling them?
What did the first book teach you to distrust about official explanations?

profiles.title: Les Misérables
profiles.author: Victor Hugo
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic and historical statements checked against individually listed sources. Original interpretations are explicitly editorial. No full-text audit, exhaustive trigger list, exact reader copy or cover verification.

publication.basis: Original French book publication 1862, distinct from Hapgood’s 1887 English translation.

profiles.genre_and_form: French social/historical novel translated into English; sprawling five-part narrative

series.name: Standalone work
series.sequence_status: No numbered fictional series applies to this work.

profiles.summary: Victor Hugo follows the former prisoner Jean Valjean through a society that often refuses people a second chance. The novel moves from a bishop’s act of mercy toward questions of poverty, law, childhood, revolution, conscience and love. Digressions on history, faith, urban infrastructure and politics enlarge the cast’s private dilemmas into a portrait of nineteenth-century French social life.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Les Misérables was first published in French in 1862. The reader selected an unabridged English text translated by Isabel F. Hapgood; Project Gutenberg hosts a Hapgood text with an 1887 translation attribution. The saved Les Mis daily calendar contains 365 individual chapters, original French titles, Hapgood English headings and attributed user-supplied Reading Companion materials, but no modern physical edition/ISBN has been independently matched.
profiles.before_reading: An evening chapter asks for attention rather than marathon stamina. Keep the preface and occasional long digressions as part of Hugo’s project; look for how each social argument relates to the story’s question of who deserves care. The 2025 external commentary is a separate interpretive voice and should remain collapsed until after the day’s chapter.
profiles.literary_approach: Hugo alternates intimate moral scenes with panoramic social exposition, addresses to readers and highly specific accounts of people and institutions. The five volume arrangement invites a daily reading practice without requiring every chapter to serve the same narrative function.
profiles.context: The historical 1832 Paris uprising should not be confused with the French Revolution of 1789, despite errors in some modern retail blurbs. A nineteenth-century novel may blend identifiable events with invented actions. “365 chapters” describes the preserved reader-selected schedule, not a guarantee that every print/abridged edition has the same segmentation.

themes.label: Mercy and institutions
themes.discussion: Individual compassion can expose failures in supposedly neutral rules.

themes.label: Social responsibility
themes.discussion: Hugo links poverty and education to moral opportunity.

themes.label: Digression as argument
themes.discussion: History and infrastructure passages enlarge the stakes beyond a protagonist’s fate.

profiles.personal_fit: Ideal for reflective nightly reading with rich moral debate, detailed nineteenth-century prose and a dependable companion schedule.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The sheer scale, political essays and long historical departures from the immediate plot may be demanding when reading tired at night.

notes: Poverty, violence, imprisonment, persecution, child suffering, grief and other distressing experiences occur; this list is not exhaustive.
The daily 2025 commentary is a separate attributed interpretation and may contain spoilers if opened before reading.

When does mercy challenge a rule rather than ignore it?
What is the function of the digression you just read?
discussion_questions: Can the law be lawful yet unjust?
How does Hugo invite a reader to assign responsibility for another person’s suffering?

profiles.title: Raising Steam
profiles.author: Terry Pratchett
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic and historical statements checked against individually listed sources. Original interpretations are explicitly editorial. No full-text audit, exhaustive trigger list, exact reader copy or cover verification.

publication.basis: Verified publisher/library work-level date; editions and translated texts may carry separate dates.

profiles.genre_and_form: Comic fantasy; technology, labor and railway satire

series.name: Discworld — Moist von Lipwig novels
series.sequence_status: Third central Moist novel after Going Postal and Making Money. Discworld chronology is shared-world rather than a promise of one fixed universal reading order.

profiles.summary: A new steam engine disrupts established habits in Ankh-Morpork, attracting commercial ambition, public wonder and opposition. Moist von Lipwig is drawn into making a railroad plausible to a city that rarely does anything simply. The railway’s expansion exposes how technology reshapes relationships among species, authorities, cities and distant communities.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Pratchett’s official site lists Raising Steam in November 2013. Penguin describes it as part of Discworld’s industrial-change sequence; the official Making Money entry supplies the earlier Moist context. Later edition listings are not evidence about which copy a reader owns or a universal placement relative to every Discworld arc.
profiles.before_reading: Watch who benefits from the railway and who bears its costs. Consider the ordinary people who maintain the apparently magical transformation of transport. It may help to recall the public-institution jokes from Going Postal and Making Money, but avoid assuming the plot must be consumed in rigid series order.
profiles.literary_approach: The comic narrative juxtaposes engineering novelty with bureaucratic deal-making, labor, regional prejudice and the demands of social change. Discworld’s absurdities let ideas about public infrastructure be argued without presenting them as an economic textbook.
profiles.context: Railway history provides material for parody, but the novel’s invented political factions and goblin/dwarf groups are not simple substitutes for real-world populations. An interpretive analogy should be presented as a question, not the author’s confirmed intent.

themes.label: Innovation and cost
themes.discussion: A faster technology changes power as well as travel.

themes.label: Public works
themes.discussion: Infrastructure depends on trust, coordination and maintenance.

themes.label: Prejudice and contact
themes.discussion: Travel may bring communities together without automatically resolving disagreement.

profiles.personal_fit: An upbeat, witty later Discworld choice that still makes you think about invention, institutions and the social costs of progress.
profiles.possible_mismatch: Its crowded social world and many overlapping Discworld references may feel sprawling compared with the tight premise of Going Postal.

notes: Official premise refers to angry conflicts, threats and comic peril.
No scene-by-scene violence or other content audit was performed.

reading_questions: Who controls access to movement and information in this chapter?
What labor is invisible behind the glamour of invention?
Where does the novel side with a skeptic of progress?
discussion_questions: Does progress always create winners and losers?
How does public trust in railways compare with trust in the bank of Making Money?

related_connections.note: Earlier Moist novel on institutions and public trust.

profiles.title: The Sum of Us
profiles.author: Heather McGhee
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic and historical statements checked against individually listed sources. Original interpretations are explicitly editorial. No full-text audit, exhaustive trigger list, exact reader copy or cover verification.

publication.basis: Verified publisher/library work-level date; editions and translated texts may carry separate dates.

profiles.genre_and_form: Reported policy nonfiction and civic/economic argument

series.name: Standalone work
series.sequence_status: No numbered fictional series applies to this work.

profiles.summary: Heather McGhee asks why people support policies that can impoverish their own communities when an improvement would also help people across racial lines. Moving from public swimming pools to housing, employment and environmental policy, she describes “zero-sum” political thinking and searches for what she calls a solidarity dividend: gains enabled by cooperation rather than scarcity narratives.
profiles.author_and_work_background: One World published the original hardcover in February 2021; the paperback and other editions have separate length and publication data. The publisher describes reporting across different U.S. regions, while Publishers Weekly and Kirkus provide independent critical reception. An interview with McGhee clarifies her account of her research questions, but is not independent verification of each cause-effect conclusion.
profiles.before_reading: When you encounter an anecdote, ask what concrete policy or comparative data is used to support it. Keep examples of cooperation separate from evidence that a particular intervention caused an economic result. Notice where the book speaks in a political recommendation rather than a measured estimate.
profiles.literary_approach: A travel-and-interview structure allows a complex economic thesis to unfold through recognizable places and people. The drained swimming pool operates as an accessible image of the collective losses that can follow exclusionary decisions.
profiles.context: The book’s zero-sum account is a broad interpretive framework for American policy. It is a claim to assess alongside competing explanations for deindustrialization, public disinvestment and inequality, not a universal one-factor proof of every historical development.

themes.label: Zero-sum politics
themes.discussion: The book questions the premise that collective gain must be someone else’s loss.

themes.label: Public goods
themes.discussion: Shared institutions can become more fragile when access is denied.

themes.label: Solidarity dividend
themes.discussion: Cross-group cooperation is framed as practical self-interest as well as moral action.

profiles.personal_fit: Useful for tying ethical reading to tangible policy and economics, and particularly strong as a comparative companion to Alexander and Wilkerson.
profiles.possible_mismatch: A persuasive narrative can move faster than underlying causal identification; economic or historical generalizations deserve source-by-source review before being repeated as settled.

notes: Racism, historical exclusion, economic hardship and policy harm are central; no exhaustive sensitive-content review was done.
Examples are historically situated around the 2021 publication and may need updated policy checks.

reading_questions: What is the mechanism between racial division and a public cost here?
Which claim has a source you could independently verify?
Where does the interview convey testimony rather than a controlled study?
discussion_questions: Does solidarity require shared identity or merely overlapping interests?
When is the “zero-sum” metaphor helpful and when might a genuine scarce resource complicate it?

related_connections.label: The New Jim Crow
related_connections.note: Compare the institutional harm of criminal punishment with broader public investment arguments.

related_connections.label: Caste
related_connections.note: Compare structural hierarchy with coalition-building interventions.

profiles.title: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
profiles.author: Immanuel Kant
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic and historical statements checked against individually listed sources. Original interpretations are explicitly editorial. No full-text audit, exhaustive trigger list, exact reader copy or cover verification.

publication.basis: 1785 first German publication, distinct from modern translations and scholarly editions.

profiles.genre_and_form: Eighteenth-century German moral philosophy; systematic ethical argument

series.name: Standalone work
series.sequence_status: No numbered fictional series applies to this work.

profiles.summary: Kant seeks the principle that would make an action morally worthy independently of the pleasure or advantage it brings. Through the idea of a good will, duty and the categorical imperative, the Groundwork asks readers to test a maxim as a rule everyone could follow and to regard humanity as an end, not merely an instrument. The philosophical argument demands attention to how reasons justify choices.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The Groundwork first appeared in German in 1785. Cambridge’s modern edition offers Mary Gregor’s translation revised by Jens Timmermann, with Christine Korsgaard’s introduction; a bilingual German–English version illustrates how translation and editorial choices differ. The Stanford Encyclopedia examines the several formulations of Kant’s imperative and significant disputes about their relation and derivation.
profiles.before_reading: Read slowly enough to write a maxim of your own before deciding whether it could be universal. Distinguish Kant’s argument from the simplified slogan “do your duty.” Use a glossary for terms such as good will, autonomy, inclination and hypothetical imperative; mark where different translators might make a sentence sound more absolute.
profiles.literary_approach: The book develops an abstract argument in stages rather than telling a story. Kant uses contrasting examples of action from duty versus conformity to duty, then moves from an account of rational agency toward an unconditional principle. One sentence can carry several assumptions worth unpacking.
profiles.context: Kant’s Enlightenment philosophy has a complicated historical reception and live interpretive disagreements. Modern scholars question the relationship between formulations of the categorical imperative, motivational psychology and applications to actual duties; the Groundwork is not a self-evident checklist.

themes.label: Good will and motive
themes.discussion: For Kant the basis of moral worth is not a favorable outcome alone.

themes.label: Universalizability
themes.discussion: A reason for acting must be tested beyond its convenience to one person.

themes.label: Humanity as an end
themes.discussion: People are not merely useful tools for achieving somebody else’s purpose.

profiles.personal_fit: A major anchor for required philosophy reading and meaningful discussion of ethical consistency; combines naturally with Aristotle and Epictetus.
profiles.possible_mismatch: Dense eighteenth-century argument and technical translation choices can feel austere; reading a summary alone risks missing disputed steps in the reasoning.

notes: Historical discussion of self-harm and hard moral examples may appear in modern editions; no exhaustive edition-specific audit was conducted.
Do not treat Kant’s hypothetical cases as medical, legal or mental-health advice.

reading_questions: What exact maxim is being proposed here?
Does the example show an action is good or that a reason for it is good?
Which step needs a premise Kant has not yet defended?
discussion_questions: Do the universal-law and humanity formulations always give the same judgment?
Can rigid duties adequately account for competing moral commitments?

related_connections.label: Nicomachean Ethics
related_connections.note: Contrast virtue and flourishing with duty and categorical law.

related_connections.label: The Enchiridion
related_connections.note: Explore rival ancient and modern accounts of rational agency.
